definition: Grammar induction (or grammatical inference) is the process in machine learning of learning a formal grammar (usually as a collection of re-write rules or productions or alternatively as a finite-state machine or automaton of some kind) from a set of observations, thus constructing a model which accounts for the characteristics of the observed objects.
details: More generally, grammatical inference is that branch of machine learning where the instance space consists of discrete combinatorial objects such as strings, trees and graphs.

explainer.lead: Grammar induction learns a compact set of rules that could have produced a collection of observed examples. It turns strings, trees, or graphs into a model of their structure, rather than requiring someone to write every rule by hand.

tiers.eli5: Imagine seeing several necklaces made from coloured beads and figuring out the pattern used to make them. Grammar induction does something similar: it looks at examples and works out rules that describe how their pieces fit together.
tiers.practitioner: Apply it when observations are discrete structures such as strings, trees, or graphs and the desired output is an interpretable structural model. Choose a representation such as rewrite rules or a finite-state automaton, then check whether the learned model accounts for the observed examples rather than merely storing them.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a set of observations O from an instance space of discrete combinatorial objects, grammatical inference learns a formal grammar G, typically a set of productions, or an automaton A that models characteristics of O. The instance space may contain strings, trees, or graphs.

explainer.example: From the strings ab, aabb, and aaabbb, a learner could infer the productions S -> aSb and S -> the empty string. These rules generate equal numbers of a's and b's, with every a before every b, and also account for all three observations.

usedIn.name: String structure learning
usedIn.detail: Learning rewrite rules or automata from observed strings.

usedIn.name: Tree structure learning
usedIn.detail: Modelling observations whose instances are trees.

usedIn.name: Graph structure learning
usedIn.detail: Modelling observations whose instances are graphs.

explainer.intuition: A grammar is a recipe for building structured objects, and induction means working backwards from finished objects to a recipe. The learned recipe should account for the patterns visible in the observations.
howItWorks: Collect observations such as strings, trees, or graphs.
Choose a model form: productions or an automaton.
Infer rules or transitions that fit the observations.
Use the resulting grammar as a model of their structure.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a way to learn explicit structural models from examples instead of constructing every grammar manually. The result can be a set of productions or an automaton, depending on the chosen representation.
misconceptions: It learns a grammar from observations; it is not simply handwriting one.
It is not limited to strings: trees and graphs can also be instances.

diagram.caption: Grammar induction turns observations and a chosen model representation into a learned structural model.
